pride_data.title: LC-MS/MS analysis of Gd-IgA1 and secretary TfR1 cross-linked complex
pride_data.projectDescription: The retention of galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) in the glomerular mesangium is a hallmark of IgA nephropathy (IgAN). The immune complex formed by Gd-IgA1 binds to transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) and deposits on mesangial cell, inducing cell proliferation, inflammatory response, matrix secretion, etc., causes organic damage and dysfunction of the kidney. Even though, the mechanism of how Gd-IgA1 recognize and bind to TfR1 is unclear.  In this experiment, we ami to determine the specific interaction region responsible for Gd-IgA1 and TfR1. We prepared a complex of Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 by incubating the two proteins under acidic conditions and stabilizing it using the chemical cross-linking agent glutaraldehyde. And then, the gel bands corresponding to the Gd-IgA1-TfR1 complex was exexcised from the SDS-PAGE gel and analyzed by high-resolution mass spectrometry. This analysis identified fragments containing the hinge peptide sequence, with the R276 residue interacting with the E350 and D356 residues in the apical domain of TfR1. Our results reveal that the hinge peptide of Gd-IgA1 interacts specifically with the apical domain of TfR1.
pride_data.sampleProcessingProtocol: purified TfR1 protein was mixed with Gd-IgA1 at a molar ratio of 1:3 in buffer A (pH 5.5) and incubated at room temperature for 2 hours. After that, the 1-Ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl) carbodiimide (EDC) and N-Hydroxysulfosuccinimide (sulfo-NHS) solutions (Cytiva, BR100050) were mixed with a ratio of (1:5, v: v) and transferred to the protein mixture at a ratio of (1:10, v: v) drop by drop. The sample continued to incubate under room temperature for another 2 hours, and then equal volume of 100mM tris buffer (pH 5.5) was used to end the crosslinking reaction. 100 μL samples (about 50-60μg proteins) were denatured by adding 20 μL 5 loading buffer and treated in 100 ℃ heating, and then separated by SDS-PAGE with a gradient gel (4-15%). The Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 crosslinked band in the gel was cut and analyzed by mass spectrometry.
pride_data.dataProcessingProtocol: Liquid Chromatography Tandem Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a High-Energy Collisional Dissociation (HCD) fragmentation function was employed for LC-MS/MS analyses. The gel samples were firstly cut into little pieces (~1 mm3) and incubated in 50 mM NH4HCO3/acetonitrile solution (1:1, v: v) to destain. Then the gel was washed using 100% acetonitrile for 2 times and dehydrated in vacuum. The samples were treated with DTT and IAA to reductive alkylation. Protein digested using trypsin overnight, and peptides were recollected and concentrated using a vacuum concentrator. In LC-MS/MS analysis, digested products were separated by a 120 min gradient elution at a flow rate 0.300 µL/min with the Thermo Ultimate 3000 nano-UPLC system which was directly interfaced with the Thermo Fusion LUMOS mass spectrometer. The analytical column was an Acclaim PepMap RSLC column (75 µm ID, 250 mm length, C18). Mobile phase A consisted of 0.1% formic acid, and mobile phase B consisted of 100% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid. The Fusion LUMOS mass spectrometer was operated in the data-dependent acquisition mode using Xcalibur 4.1.50 software and there is a single full-scan mass spectrum in the Orbitrap (375-1500 m/z, 60,000 resolution) followed by data-dependent MS/MS scans. The MS/MS spectra from each LC-MS/MS run were searched against the selected database using the software Byonic.

passages.text: Lysosome-mediated aggregation of galactose-deficient IgA1 with transferrin receptor 1 links to IgA nephropathy

The retention of galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) in the mesangium is central to IgA nephropathy (IgAN), but its intracellular fate remains unclear. Here, we show that transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) mediates Gd-IgA1 uptake into mesangial cell lysosomes, where it forms non-digestible aggregates, disrupts lysosomal function, and triggers inflammatory responses. In renal biopsies from IgAN patients, IgA1 aggregates co-localize with TfR1 within lysosomes. In male mice, TfR1 overexpression enhanced lysosomal accumulation of Gd-IgA1, whereas TfR1 knockdown reduced it. Mechanistically, acidic pH strengthens TfR1–Gd-IgA1 binding via the galactose-deficient hinge region and residue R276. While we acknowledge that sialylation commonly found in patient-derived IgA1 might influence TfR1 binding and that other receptors, such as ASGPR, were not evaluated, our findings nonetheless reveal a lysosome-centered mechanism in IgAN and highlight receptor-mediated retention of Gd-IgA1 as a potential therapeutic target.

The retention of galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) in the mesangium leads to pathogenesis in IgA nephropathy. Here the authors report that Gd-IgA1 is internalized by mesangial cells potentially via transferrin receptor 1, forming aggregates that disrupt lysosomal function and elicit inflammation.
Introduction

IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common primary glomerulonephritis and a major cause of end-stage kidney disease. The pathological hallmark of IgAN is the deposition of predominantly IgA1 immune complexes in the mesangium, but the mechanisms underlying the abnormal deposition of IgA1 in the kidneys remain unclear.

Galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) is a key factor in the pathogenesis of IgAN, serving as the initiating event in the “multi-hit” hypothesis. Our previous research has demonstrated that galactose-deficiency enhances IgA1 deposition, and this stable deposition of Gd-IgA1 can lead to proteinuria. Furthermore, the biological events that follow the entry of Gd-IgA1 into the mesangial area are poorly understood. Previous studies indicated that the deposition site of electron-dense deposits (EDDs), primarily composed of IgA1, was extracellular to mesangial cells, with inadequate evidence supporting mesangial cell uptake of EDDs. Given that mesangial cells possess active internalization properties, they are likely crucial for the degradation of Gd-IgA1. Clarifying these biological events, particularly the mechanisms by which that Gd-IgA1 accumulated in mesangial area is essential for uncovering the mystery of IgAN.

Mesangial cells are located between the capillaries of the glomeruli, where they provide structural support, regulate blood flow, and play a crucial role in immune responses by clearing immune complexes and other particles through endocytosis and lysosomal activity. Endocytosis is a process by which cells internalize external substances into vesicles that are subsequently transported to lysosomes for degradation. Lysosomes act as cellular recycling centers, with acidic compartments containing over 60 distinct hydrolases in mammalian cells. They are also critical to cellular metabolism and immune responses. However, under pathological conditions, lysosomes can become repositories for aberrant substances. For example, in Alzheimer’s disease, the accumulation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) within lysosomes leads to their dysfunction. Similarly, in IgAN, an excess of circulating Gd-IgA1 may be sequestered within the lysosomes of mesangial cells, potentially triggering glomerular injury. Therefore, further investigation into the mechanisms of Gd-IgA1 uptake by mesangial cells and its lysosomal processing is warranted.

The transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) has been recognized as a receptor for mesangial cell binding with IgA1 and plays a pathological role in IgAN. Moura et al. first identified TfR1 as a novel receptor for IgA1 and observed its enhanced expression on mesangial cells in IgAN, suggesting a significant role in disease pathogenesis. Subsequent studies revealed that engagement of TfR1 by polymeric IgA1 induces a positive feedback loop, characterized by increased receptor expression and mesangial cell proliferation, thereby exacerbating disease progression. Further evidence demonstrated that the interaction between polymeric IgA1 and TfR1 drives mesangial cell proliferation, linking receptor engagement to cellular responses in IgAN. Here, we investigated how TfR1 mediates the lysosomal entry of Gd-IgA1 in mesangial cells, leading to lysosomal dysfunction and inflammatory responses. Furthermore, we explored how the acidic intra-lysosomal environment influences the molecular dynamics of the interaction between Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 and identified the critical role of the galactose-deficient hinge region of Gd-IgA1 in its binding affinity to TfR1. These findings provide crucial insights into the mechanisms underlying the abnormal accumulation of Gd-IgA1 in the mesangium and its pathological consequences.

To obtain a comprehensive spatial landscape of mesangial cells and IgA1 deposition in the kidneys of IgAN patients, we conducted volumetric electron microscopy (EM) on renal tissues from IgAN patients. Conventional renal EM pathology involves sampling at an extremely limited plane, with EM sections being 80 nanometers thick and glomerular diameters measuring 200 micrometers. Each EM image corresponds to roughly a 4 ‱ (permyriad) sampling, often neglecting complete spatial information. To perform volumetric EM, we sectioned at a thickness of 50 nanometers, acquiring 1300 serial sections of images. Through three-dimensional reconstruction, we discovered numerous lysosomes with prominent densities and sizes, providing a more detailed spatial understanding of their distribution and morphology (Fig. 1a). We examined the lysosome diameters and density in the renal EM pathology images from IgAN patients and para-tumoral controls, finding that the lysosomes in IgAN patients were larger and denser (Fig. 1b). Using serial sections, we performed both transmission EM and IgA1 immuno-EM on the same lysosomal region of the mesangial cells, revealing the deposition of gold-labeled IgA1 within the lysosomes of IgAN patients (Fig. 1c). Notably, although it is widely accepted that electron-dense deposits (EDD) formed by IgA1 are located outside the mesangial cells, our immuno-EM analysis revealed that IgA1 proteins can aggregate within the lysosomes of renal mesangial cells, as evidenced by the encapsulation of IgA1 within single-membrane structures that were positively labeled for lysosomal marker LAMP1 by immuno-EM (Fig. 1d, e). Immunofluorescence examinations further confirmed the co-localization of the LAMP1 and IgA1 in the mesangial area of IgAN patients (Fig. 1f). These results indicate that IgA1 can be retained within the lysosomes of mesangial cells in IgAN patients, offering new spatial distribution insights into IgA1 deposition under pathological conditions of IgAN.

To elucidate the biological events during mesangial cells uptake of IgA1 proteins, we labeled Gd-IgA1 protein with Alexa Fluor® 647 dye (AF647) and labeled the endosomes and lysosomes of mesangial cells with green fluorescent protein (GFP), then incubated them with human mesangial cells. We used Gd-IgA1 because it is recognized as the main pathological IgA1 leading to IgAN, and our previous studies using multi-model intravital imaging showed stronger renal deposition of Gd-IgA1. First, we verified that Gd-IgA1 does not spontaneously form aggregates. Additionally, the size and galactose deficiency of the Gd-IgA1 protein were not affected by conjugation with AF647 (Supplementary Fig. 1a–d). Using high-intensity structured illumination microscopy (HIS-SIM), a live-cell super-resolution imaging method, we tracked the localization of Gd-IgA1 in different cellular compartments of mesangial cells. Gd-IgA1 gradually entered early endosomes and late endosomes, then fused with lysosomes and stabilized in lysosomes (Fig. 2a). Cellular electron microscopy confirmed a significant increase in lysosomes within mesangial cells following Gd-IgA1 incubation (Fig. 2b). This finding is not only consistent with the pathological findings in patients with IgAN, indicating that human mesangial cells have a strong capacity to uptake Gd-IgA1 proteins, but also demonstrates that Gd-IgA1 might be favorable for endocytosis by mesangial cells and hence accumulate within lysosomes.

These results prompted us to investigate the mechanism of Gd-IgA1 deposition in the lysosomes of mesangial cells. We employed flow cytometry experiments, which revealed a significantly greater binding of Gd-IgA1 to mesangial cells, compared with IgA1 with normal galactosylation (HC-IgA1), and the binding was concentration-dependent (Fig. 2c). This result suggested that the binding of Gd-IgA1 to mesangial cells is mediated by membrane proteins/receptors on mesangial cells. To identify such receptors, we used a CRISPR-Cas9 based screening strategy, utilizing a library containing ~2600 membrane proteins. We obtained a list of candidate genes by sequencing sgRNAs from the population of mesangial cells with the lowest 10% binding affinity to Gd-IgA1 (Fig. 2d, e). To identify the most likely candidate, we performed siRNA knockdowns on the receptors in the list, followed by flow cytometry binding assays. We found that Tfrc was among these candidates, and knocking down Tfrc significantly inhibited the binding of Gd-IgA1 to mesangial cells (Fig. 2f), suggesting that TfR1 is a critical receptor mediating the interaction between mesangial cells and Gd-IgA1.

Live-cell imaging revealed that human mesangial cells expressing TfR1-GFP internalized Gd-IgA1 protein, and Gd-IgA1 co-localized with TfR1 in vesicles (Fig. 3a). Based on these findings, we generated stable cell lines overexpressing or knocked down for TFRC using human mesangial cells (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). Over-expression of TfR1 significantly enhanced Gd-IgA1 endocytosis, whereas knocking down TfR1 significantly inhibited this process in human mesangial cells (Fig. 3c). We performed a series of experiments with graded knockdown or overexpression of TfR1 in mesangial cells and found that the binding of Gd-IgA1 to mesangial cells was consistent with the levels of TfR1 expression (Fig. 3d–g). We introduced the TfR1 inhibitor Ferristatin II to reduce TfR1 expression and found that Ferristatin II significantly inhibited the binding of Gd-IgA1 to mesangial cells (Fig. 3h, i). In summary, these findings demonstrate that TfR1 mediates the binding and endocytosis of Gd-IgA1 by mesangial cells.

Following our observations that TfR1 mediated the endocytosis of Gd-IgA1 into mesangial cells, we next examined the fate of Gd-IgA1 within lysosomes and its impact on cellular function and inflammation. First, we assessed the degradation rate of Gd-IgA1 in lysosomes. After 48 h, mesangial cells degraded HC-IgA1, whereas Gd-IgA1 remained accumulated within the lysosomes (Fig. 4a, b). ELISA quantification confirmed a significantly higher concentration of Gd-IgA1 within mesangial cells compared to HC-IgA1 (Fig. 4c). Non-reducing immunoblots further demonstrated that intact Gd-IgA1 was retained in mesangial cells (Fig. 4d), suggesting impaired degradation of Gd-IgA1 within lysosomes. To further understand the role of TfR1 in this process, we knocked down TfR1 in mesangial cells and observed a significant reduction in the retention of Gd-IgA1 within these cells (Fig. 4e–g). Furthermore, Ferristatin II also inhibited the accumulation of Gd-IgA1 in mesangial cells (Fig. 4h–j), supporting the hypothesis that TfR1 mediates the entry and subsequent retention of Gd-IgA1 in lysosomes.

Using an aggresome detection assay, we observed the formation of spherical and globular protein aggregates within mesangial cells following Gd-IgA1 incubation (Fig. 5a). These aggregates co-localized with IgA1, indicating that Gd-IgA1 formed protein aggregates after entry into the lysosomes of mesangial cells (Fig. 5b). To assess lysosomal function, we employed a cellular lysosome detection assay, where the fluorescence signal generated by degradation is proportional to intracellular lysosomal activity. Our results showed that the fluorescence signal in mesangial cells treated with Gd-IgA1 was significantly suppressed, indicating that Gd-IgA1 inhibits lysosomal function more effectively than known lysosomal inhibitors (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Fig. 3). This lysosomal dysfunction was linked to the aggregation of Gd-IgA1, impairing the cell’s ability to degrade these proteins. TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis was significantly reduced by Gd-IgA1 retention (Fig. 5d). The levels of the lysosomal protease cathepsin B and cathepsin D were also significantly reduced (Fig. 5e). These results indicated that lysosomal function was inhibited by Gd-IgA1 retention.

In parallel, an inflammatory cytokine array analysis showed a significant increase in IL6, CXCL8/ IL-8, CCL3/ MIP-1α and TNF-α levels in mesangial cells upon stimulation with Gd-IgA1 (Fig. 5f, g). This finding was further validated by ELISA, which demonstrated a significant increase in IL-6 secretion by mesangial cells upon Gd-IgA1 stimulation (Fig. 5h). Together, these results suggest that TfR1 mediates the accumulation of Gd-IgA1 in lysosomes, leading to the formation of protein aggregates and subsequent lysosomal dysfunction. This dysfunction triggers inflammatory responses in mesangial cells, suggesting a novel pathogenic mechanism in IgAN.

To validate our in vitro findings on the role of TfR1 in mediating Gd-IgA1 endocytosis and its subsequent effects in vivo, we conducted experiments involving TfR1 overexpression and knockdown in BALB/c Nude mice. Firstly, we overexpressed TfR1 in nude mice by intravenously injecting an AAV9-Tfrc virus (2 × 1010 GC/g bodyweight). Separately, we knocked down TfR1 in mice using an AAV9-shTfrc virus (4 × 1010 GC/g bodyweight). The efficiency of TfR1 overexpression and knockdown was confirmed through western blotting and immunofluorescent assessment (Supplementary Fig. 4a–d). We then dynamically monitored the intensity of Gd-IgA1 deposition in the kidneys using in vivo fluorescence imaging. A significant increase in Gd-IgA1 deposition was observed in the kidneys of mice overexpressing TfR1, whereas TfR1 knockdown significantly inhibited Gd-IgA1 deposition in the kidneys (Fig. 6a, b). Immunofluorescent examinations on frozen sections of renal tissue confirmed an increase in the deposition of Gd-IgA1 in the mesangial cells of mice with TfR1 overexpression (Supplementary Fig. 4e). Gd-IgA1 was colocalized with LAMP1 and TfR1, demonstrating the precise subcellular location of Gd-IgA1 deposition within the lysosomes of mesangial cells (Fig. 6c). This result suggested that TfR1 enhances the deposition of Gd-IgA1 in the lysosomes of mesangial cells, corroborating our in vitro findings. Subsequently, immunofluorescence staining confirmed reduced deposition of Gd-IgA1 in the TfR1 knockdown group (Fig. 6d, Supplementary Fig. 4f). These findings reinforced the critical role of TfR1 in mediating the endocytosis and lysosomal deposition of Gd-IgA1 in mesangial cells, as observed in our in vitro studies, demonstrating that TfR1 overexpression exacerbates, while TfR1 knockdown mitigates, Gd-IgA1 accumulation in the mouse model.

To further elucidate the role of TfR1 in patients with IgAN, we examined TfR1 expression in renal samples from patients with IgAN. Immunofluorescence staining revealed co-localization of TfR1 and IgA1 protein in the mesangium of glomeruli in IgAN patients (Fig. 7a). This observation is consistent with our cellular experiments, supporting the notion that TfR1 mediates the binding of IgA1 to mesangial cells in IgAN patients. Immunohistochemistry further demonstrated a significant increase in TfR1 expression in the glomeruli of IgAN patients compared to controls (Fig. 7b). This finding aligns with our in vitro data, suggesting that elevated TfR1 expression is a characteristic feature of IgAN.

Using RNAscope assay, we identified that mesangial cells express TfR1 mRNA, predominantly in cells positive for alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), indicating high in situ expression of TfR1 in mesangial cells of IgAN patients (Fig. 7c). This high expression of TfR1 mRNA in mesangial cells correlates with our previous findings on its role in mediating Gd-IgA1 endocytosis and deposition. Moreover, we discovered a significant correlation between the expression level of glomerular mesangial TfR1 and urinary protein levels in IgAN patients (R = 0.398, P < 0.0001, Fig. 7d, Supplementary table 1). This suggests that the degree of TfR1 expression is associated with the severity of kidney damage in these patients, indicating a potential prognostic value of TfR1 expression in IgAN.

In summary, these findings in patient samples strengthen the critical role of TfR1 in mediating the endocytosis and lysosomal deposition of Gd-IgA1 in mesangial cells, as demonstrated in our in vitro and mouse models. The significant increase in TfR1 expression and its correlation with disease severity in IgAN patients underscore the potential of targeting TfR1 as a therapeutic strategy.

To investigate how Gd-IgA1 interacts with TfR1, we recombinantly expressed and purified IgA1 in HEK293 cells and prepared Gd-IgA1 using glycosidases (including α2-3, 6, 8 neuraminidase, and β1-3 galactosidase). The successful preparation of Gd-IgA1 was confirmed via western blotting with anti-IgA1 and anti-Gd-IgA1 antibodies (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b). We then examined the affinity between Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 under various conditions using surface plasmon resonance (SPR). Under physiological conditions (150 mM NaCl, pH 7.2), Gd-IgA1 demonstrated a higher binding capacity to TfR1 compared to HC-IgA1, which is critical for the initial endocytosis process, though this binding was still weaker than that of transferrin (supplementary Table 2). Notably, under acidic conditions (pH 5.5), the binding capacity of Gd-IgA1 to TfR1 significantly increased, mirroring the behavior of the positive control, transferrin (Apo state). These findings strongly suggest that acidic conditions play a key role in regulating the Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 interaction. To further explore this, we measured the affinity of Gd-IgA1 to TfR1 under pH 5.5 conditions, finding a binding capacity of KD = 1.09 × 10-6 M (Fig. 8a). This result indicates the interaction between Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 in acidic environments, likely contributing to the formation of degradation-resistant complexes.

To further confirm the clinical relevance of these findings, we incubated TfR1 coupled beads with IgA1 from IgAN patients in 100 mM Hepes buffer at pH 7.2 or pH 5.5. Consistent with the SPR results, more intense IgA1 signal was detected binding to TfR1 beads under pH 5.5, whereas minimal IgA1 binding to TfR1 was detected under pH 7.2 conditions (Supplementary Fig. 5c).

To understand the impact of acidic conditions on the interaction between Gd-IgA1 and TfR1, we assessed the binding capacity of Gd-IgA1 to TfR1 under a range of acidic pH conditions. Interestingly, as the buffer pH was decreased from 7.2 to 5.0, both the binding levels and stability of Gd-IgA1 progressively increased (supplementary Table 3), indicating a continuous increase in affinity between Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 from neutral to acidic conditions. These data support that acidic conditions within lysosomes enable Gd-IgA1 to acquire higher affinity for TfR1, promoting the formation of large complexes (aggregates). This aggregation leads to incomplete degradation and lysosomal deposition of Gd-IgA1. Thus, the increased binding affinity of Gd-IgA1 to TfR1 under acidic conditions highlights a crucial aspect of IgAN pathogenesis.

Next, we aimed to determine the specific interaction region responsible for Gd-IgA1 and TfR1. We prepared a complex of Gd-IgA1 and extracellular domain of TfR1 by incubating the two proteins under acidic conditions and stabilizing it using the chemical cross-linking agent glutaraldehyde (Fig. 8b). A stable Gd-IgA1-TfR1 complex was obtained through size exclusion chromatography (Fig. 8c). The peak of this complex was distinct, with molecular weights matching the expected mass, and the peak of the Gd-IgA1-TfR1 complex appeared ahead of the separate peaks of TfR1 or Gd-IgA1. This observation suggests that Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 form a stable complex, and their combined mass is greater than the individual proteins, indicating successful complex formation. Under negative staining transmission electron microscopy, the protein particles of the Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 complex were clear and uniform in response to uranyl salts (Fig. 8d). This indicates that the interaction between Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 is stable. More importantly, in western blot analysis, in addition to detecting Gd-IgA1 (heavy chain, ~55 kDa) and extracellular domain of TfR1 (~77 kDa), we detected complex of TfR1 and the heavy chain of Gd-IgA1 (~132 kDa) using anti-Flag antibody (Supplementary Fig. 6a). Since deglycosidase removed O-glycosylation from the hinge peptide, these results suggest that TfR1 likely interacted with Gd-IgA1 through the galactose-deficient hinge peptide.

To test the hypothesis that the hinge peptide of Gd-IgA1 is the binding site for TfR1, we excised the gel bands corresponding to the Gd-IgA1-TfR1 complex from the SDS-PAGE gel and analyzed them by high-resolution mass spectrometry (Fig. 9a). This analysis identified fragments containing the hinge peptide sequence, with the R276 residue interacting with the E350 and D356 residues in the apical domain of TfR1 (Fig. 9b, Supplementary Fig. 6b; supplementary Table 4). These results reveal that the hinge peptide of Gd-IgA1 interacts specifically with the apical domain of TfR1.

To further investigate the impact of the specific site R276 near the IgA1 hinge peptide on its binding to TfR1, we prepared two types of hinge peptides. The short hinge peptide (short-HP) included only the hinge peptide domain (V253-S271), while the long hinge peptide (long-HP) encompassed both the hinge peptide domain and the adjacent C-terminal sequence (C272-R276) (Fig. 9c). We tested the binding affinity of these peptides to TfR1 under various pH conditions. The binding level of short-HP remained low and unchanged across different pH levels, similar to the negative control Flag peptide (supplementary Table 5). In contrast, the binding capacity of long-HP to TfR1 increased in a pH 5.5 buffer, mirroring the behavior of the full-length Gd-IgA1 protein. This finding highlights the critical role of the adjacent C-terminal sequence (C272-R276) in the interaction between IgA1 and TfR1, particularly under acidic conditions. In the kinetic affinity assay, the long-HP peptide exhibited a slow association and fast dissociation pattern (Fig. 9d). Its affinity index (KD = 5.158 × 10-5 M), although lower than that of the full-length Gd-IgA1 protein, is within the affinity range typical for many small molecules with their receptors. We further synthesized hinge peptide with N-Acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) modifications (Supplementary Fig. 7). Although the overall binding affinity did not change, the binding mode shifted to a slow association and slow dissociation pattern. This suggests that galactose-deficient modification may promote a more stable interaction between IgA1 and TfR1(Fig. 9e). In summary, the R276 site, along with the galactose-deficient IgA1 hinge peptide, is essential for binding to TfR1 under acidic conditions. These insights deepen our understanding of the molecular interactions driving Gd-IgA1 deposition and suggest potential therapeutic targets for inhibiting the Gd-IgA1-TfR1 interaction to alleviate IgAN.
Discussion

Studies have demonstrated that the Gd-IgA1 interacting with receptors on the mesangial cells contributes to the formation of immune deposits. While there are several identified IgA receptors, FcαRI (CD89) and TfR1 (CD71) are implicated in the deposition of Gd-IgA1 in the mesangium. Transgenic mice expressing FcαRI or those administered soluble FcαRI intravenously exhibit clinical features and kidney damage reminiscent of IgAN, suggesting a potential role for the Gd-IgA1-soluble FcαRI complex in the disease’s pathogenesis. TfR1 expression is typically low or undetectable in the glomeruli of healthy kidneys. Nonetheless, in renal biopsies from individuals with IgAN, a significant co-localization of IgA deposits with TfR1 is observed in the mesangial area (Fig. 7). The binding ability of different types of IgA1 to TfR1 depends on the glycosylation patterns and molecular weight of IgA1, suggesting that the interaction between TfR1 and Gd-IgA1 is more in line with the disease process. However, the mechanisms by which TfR1 interacts with Gd-IgA1 and facilitates its deposition in the kidney are not yet fully understood. In this study, we discovered that TfR1 mediates the internalization of Gd-IgA1 into lysosomes of mesangial cells. The subsequent accumulation of Gd-IgA1 within lysosomes induces lysosomal dysfunction and triggers inflammatory responses in mesangial cells.

Research on lysosomes in kidney disease has been limited, yet our study provides crucial insights by demonstrating that Gd-IgA1 accumulates as aggregates within the lysosomes of renal mesangial cells, leading to lysosomal dysfunction. This finding is significant for two reasons: First, the acidic environment of lysosomes enhances the binding and aggregation of the Gd-IgA1-TfR1 complex, which in turn prevents the degradation of Gd-IgA1 proteins. Second, while it has been commonly believed that Gd-IgA1 is deposited extracellularly in the form of EDD in the mesangial area, our research suggests an alternative or complementary mechanism. Through cellular experiments, animal models, and patient samples, we have confirmed that Gd-IgA1 can also be deposited intracellularly, specifically within mesangial cell lysosomes. This intracellular accumulation raises the intriguing possibility that non-digested IgA-TfR1 aggregates within lysosomes might contribute to the formation of EDD observed in IgAN patients. This potential link between intracellular lysosomal aggregates and extracellular EDD formation warrants further investigation. Understanding the exact relationship between these aggregates and EDD could provide deeper insights into the pathogenesis of IgAN.

IgG is known to differ from other Ig classes due to its longer half-life, a mechanism facilitated by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn). At acidic pH (6.0-6.5), FcRn binds to the Fc region of IgG, protecting it from lysosomal degradation during cellular endocytosis. This pH-dependent interaction allows IgG to be transported across cells and released back into the bloodstream at neutral pH (7.0-7.5), thereby extending its half-life to 21–28 days. Our study reveals that under acidic conditions in lysosomes, Gd-IgA1 has a similar anti-degradation pathway, mediated by the TfR1. This mechanism likely evolved to combat microbial mucosal invasion and infection, but in the special environment of the renal mesangial area, it leads to the abnormal accumulation and aggregation of Gd-IgA1 in mesangial cell lysosomes, disrupting the degradative functions of mesangial cells and subsequently inducing renal cell inflammatory responses.

Our study had several limitations despite the positive results. While galactose deficiency is known to induce abnormal mesangial deposition of Gd-IgA1, sialic acid modification of GalNac may also impact the pathogenicity of Gd-IgA1. Patient-derived Gd-IgA1 often retains terminal sialic acid linked to GalNAc, and sialylation may modulate TfR1 binding affinity. Additionally, although our findings highlight a role for TfR1, we cannot exclude potential involvement of other receptors such as ASGPR, particularly given its known affinity for desialylated glycoproteins. Furthermore, we acknowledge that AAV9 does not exhibit specific tropism for mesangial cells, and only male mice were used in this study. More specific TfR1 modulation and studies including both sexes will be valuable for further elucidating the gender-specific effects and refining our understanding of TfR1’s role in Gd-IgA1 accumulation.

In conclusion, our study reveals that TfR1 mediates the binding and endocytosis of Gd-IgA1 in mesangial cells, leading to its accumulation within lysosomes and subsequent lysosomal dysfunction and inflammation. The acidic lysosomal environment significantly enhances the interaction between Gd-IgA1 and TfR1, driven by the galactose-deficient hinge region and R276 site. These findings provide critical insights into the mechanisms underlying mesangial deposition of Gd-IgA1 and highlight potential therapeutic targets for IgAN, paving the way for future research aimed at mitigating this disease.
Methods
Human samples

Collection of renal biopsy and plasma samples for this study was approved by the ethics committee of Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital (KY2023-758-01). Written informed on consent was obtained from all study participants. Renal biopsy and plasma were collected from patients with renal biopsy-proven primary IgAN, prior to drug intervention. The healthy control group for plasma sample consisted of participants aged 18–70 years old with no history of autoimmune diseases, tumors, and infectious diseases. Non-tumor renal tissue from patients with kidney cancer used as control. The Clinical and laboratory characteristics of patients with IgAN was listed in Supplementary table 1.
FIB-SEM tomography and 3D reconstruction of lysosomes of mesangial cells

Focused-ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) tomography was performed to investigate the ultrastructural organization of mesangial cells in renal tissues. The tissue blocks were initially pre-fixed in a 2% paraformaldehyde (PFA) solution for 2 h. Following pre-fixation, the samples were washed three times in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (PB) to remove any excess fixative. For primary fixation, the samples were incubated in 1% osmium tetroxide (OsO4) solution, which contained 15 mg of potassium ferrocyanide dissolved in 1 mL of 10 g/L osmic acid, at room temperature while shaking for 1 h. After primary fixation, the samples were washed three times with 0.1 M PB and three times with distilled water (ddH2O), with each wash lasting 15 min. Next, the samples were stained with 1% thiocarbohydrazide (TCH) for 30 min at 40 °C in a water bath. Following staining, the samples were washed three times with ddH2O, each wash lasting 15 min. A second fixation step with 1% osmium tetroxide aqueous solution was performed for 1 h, followed by three more washes with ddH2O, each lasting 15 min. For contrast enhancement, the samples were stained with 1% uranyl acetate aqueous solution overnight at 4 °C. After staining, the samples were washed three times with ddH2O, each wash lasting 15 min. Subsequently, the samples were stained with lead aspartate solution for 1 h at 60 °C in a water bath, followed by four washes with ddH2O, each lasting 15 min. The samples were then dehydrated through a graded series of ethanol solutions (30%, 50%, 70%, 85%, and 95%) with each step lasting 15 min. This was followed by two rounds of dehydration in 100% ethanol, each lasting 30 min, and two rounds of dehydration in pure acetone, each lasting 30 min. Finally, the samples were infiltrated with Epon 812 epoxy resin, starting with a 3:7 ratio of resin to pure acetone for 4 h, followed by a 7:3 ratio of resin to acetone for another 4 h. The samples were then infiltrated with pure resin three times, each for 4 h, and polymerized in an oven at 60 °C for 48 h. The surfaces of the resin-embedded tissues were exposed using a diamond knife on an Ultracut UCT (Leica Biosystems). The block was mounted onto an HV-8 aluminum stub (Micro Star, Tokyo, Japan). The space between the block and the stub was filled with carbon paste and then coated with a thin layer of platinum-palladium using an MC1000 ion sputter coater (Hitachi High-Technologies).

The surfaces of the resin-embedded tissues were exposed using a diamond knife on a Leica EM UC7(Leica Biosystems). The block was mounted onto an 45eMetal Block. The space between the block and the stub was filled with carbon paste and then coated with a thin layer of platinum-palladium using an Q150R S sputtering instrument(Quorum Technologies Ltd, London, UK).

The coated surface of the block was imaged with a Helios G4 UC FIB-SEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, United States) at a high acceleration voltage of 10 kV to determine the area of interest. To prevent beam damage, a platinum layer was deposited on the area of interest using a 2.5 nA beam current, where gallium ions were accelerated by a voltage of 30 kV. A trench was cut using FIB milling with a 25 nA beam current, also at 30 kV, to create a new imaging surface. Serial FIB-SEM images were acquired using Auto Slice and View imaging software (Thermo Fisher Scientific). New surfaces for serial block-face imaging were generated using FIB milling with a 0.77 nA beam current.

3D Reconstruction: The alignment of serial FIB-SEM images, segmentation of target mesangial cells, and 3D reconstruction were performed using an independently developed artificial intelligence program. 1. Automatic Segmentation with UNet: we have implemented the UNet network for the training of input data, achieving the automatic segmentation of primary tissue structures. This sophisticated deep learning model has been pivotal in delineating the intricate cellular architectures with high fidelity. 2. Isosurface Extraction via Marching Cubes: Following segmentation, we applied the marching cubes algorithm to the resultant cell structure masks to extract three-dimensional isosurface information. This methodology has been essential in capturing the volumetric contours, providing a detailed three-dimensional representation of the cellular structures. 3. Iterative Smoothing and Mesh Simplification: To refine the three-dimensional isosurfaces, we employed Taubin’s smoothing and mesh simplification techniques. These iterative processes have been key in reducing noise and complexity, enhancing the accuracy and visual quality of the reconstructed models.4. Three-Dimensional Visualization with VTK: The final step in our pipeline involves the use of the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) for rendering the smoothed models. VTK serves as a powerful engine for three-dimensional visualization, enabling us to present the cellular structures in a compelling and informative manner.
Immunoelectron microscopy (IEM)

IEM samples were processed and examined by Experimental Pathology Laboratory at KingMed Diagnostics. Tissue sampling and fixation: Renal biopsy samples were strip-like with a diameter of 1 millimeter. Tissues were fixed in a 0.5% glutaraldehyde + 4% paraformaldehyde mixed fixative for at least 4 h at 4 °C. (Alfa Aesar, Catalog No. A17876)

Washing and post-fixation: Tissues were washed with 0.1 M phosphate buffer (PB) six times, for 30 min each time, and post-fixed with 1% osmium tetroxide (prepared by dissolving 1 g of osmium tetroxide crystals (TED PELLA, Catalog No. 18456) for in 0.1 M PB 1.5–2 h at 4 °C. Following post-fixation, tissues were washed with 0.1 M PB three times, for 10 min each time.

Gradient dehydration and resin infiltration: Tissues underwent gradient dehydration using ethanol and acetone as follows: 30%, 50%, 70%, 90%, and 100% ethanol (10 min each), followed by a 1:1 mixture of 100% ethanol and 100% acetone (15 min), and 100% acetone (twice, 15 min each). Tissues were infiltrated with Epon812 resin (TED PELLA, Catalog No. GP18010) in a 1:1 mixture with 100% acetone for 3-4 h at 38 °C, followed by a 1:2 mixture for another 3-4 h at 38 °C, and finally with pure Epon812 resin for 3–4 h at 38 °C.

Embedding and polymerization: Tissues were embedded in pure Epon812 resin using embedding molds and polymerized in an electric heating drying oven (model: DHG-9075A) at 38 °C for 6 h, 60 °C for 6 h, and 80 °C for 12 h.

Semi-thin sectioning and localization: Semi-thin sections (1 μm thick) were cut using an ultramicrotome (Leica UC-7) and observed under an optical microscope (Olympus BX41) to locate suitable areas for electron microscopy observation. Renal tissue containing glomeruli was selected for ultrathin sectioning.

Ultrathin sectioning and immunoelectron microscopy labeling: Ultrathin sections (70-90 nm thick) were cut using the ultramicrotome (Leica UC-7) and mounted on 200-mesh nickel grids. Immunoelectron microscopy labeling was performed with primary antibodies (IgA1 and LAMP1, diluted 1:100 in 1% BSA) overnight at 4 °C. Excess primary antibodies were washed with 0.01 M Phosphate-Buffered Saline (PBS), and gold-conjugated secondary antibodies (diluted 1:20 in 1% BSA; EMS, Catalog No. 25109) were applied and incubated for 80 min at 37 °C. Sections were rinsed with double-distilled water to remove excess antibodies.

Double staining with uranyl acetate and lead citrate: Sections were stained with 2% uranyl acetate (prepared by dissolving 2 g of uranyl acetate in 100 mL of 70% ethanol; supplied by EMS, Catalog No. 22400) for 30 min at room temperature, followed by rinsing with double-distilled water and drying. Staining with 3% lead citrate (TED PELLA, Catalog No. 19314) prepared by dissolving 3 g of lead citrate in 100 mL of freshly boiled double-distilled water, adding 0.1 mL of 10 mol/L NaOH, and shaking until the solution clears was performed for 15 min at room temperature, followed by rinsing with double-distilled water and drying.

Observation with transmission electron microscope: Samples were observed using a transmission electron microscope (model: JEM-1400, produced by JEOL Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) at an accelerating voltage of 80 kV. Sections were located at low magnification on the fluorescent screen, and the CCD camera (model: MORADA, brand: EMSIS) was inserted. The Radius ALL 2.2 (Build 21230) software was used for imaging and measurement. Microscope settings were adjusted for clear images, and images were acquired.
CRISPR-Cas9 screening

Firstly, to generate SV40 MES13-Cas9 overexpression cell lines, lentiviruses were produced by transfecting 293 T cells with Lenti-CRISPR-V2 Cas9-GFP, psPAX2 and VSV-G plasmids. SV40 MES13 cells were infected with lentivirus and GFP+ cells were selected by fluorescence-activated cell sorting. Secondly, to generate SV40 MES13 sgRNA library cell lines, retroviruses were produced by transfecting platE cells with pMXs sgRNA-library-BFP, pcl-10Al plasmids. SV40 MES13-Cas9 cells were infected with retrovirus and the virus titer was controlled to be <30%. Thirdly, the infected SV40 MES13 cells were collected and stained with 100 ug/ml Gd-IgA1-AF647 at 4°C for 30 min. Then, the 10% AF647+ or AF647- cells with Lenti-CRISPR-V2 Cas9-GFP and sgRNA-library-BFP double positive cell populations were sorted after washed by PBS. The GFP and BFP double positive cells were collected as input control. Finally, cell DNA was extracted and high-throughput sequencing was performed to detect the abundance of different sgRNA. The top 10 genes with the smallest P-values were selected as candidates. The P-values were obtained using the Model-based Analysis of Genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 Knockout (MAGeCK) method for prioritizing single-guide RNAs, genes, and pathways in genome-scale CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screens.

Cell culture

Mouse mesangial cell line SV40 MES 13 was purchased from ATCC. The base medium for this cell line is a 3:1 mixture of Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (Gibco) and Ham’s F12 medium (Gibco), both supplemented with 14 mM HEPES and fetal bovine serum at concentration of 5%. Human mesangial cells were isolated from human renal tissue and cryopreserved at passage one at 5 × 105 cells / mL (ScienCell, #4200). It was cultured with mesangial cell medium (MsCM, Cat. #4201). Incubate the cells in a humidified incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO2 to maintain optimal pH levels. Change the medium every 2–3 days to provide fresh nutrients and remove metabolic waste. Monitor the cells for confluence and passage them when they reach about 80-90% confluence to avoid overgrowth.

Construction of TFRC knockdown and overexpression mesangial cells

To generate virus for infection of mesangial cells, 2 × 105 HEK293T cells were seeded into the well of a six-well plate. Twenty-four hours later, 2 µg pLKO.1-GFP-shTfrc or 2 µg pHAGE-Tfrc-IRES-ZsGreen, 1.5 µg psPAX2 and 0.5 µg pMD2.G were mixed into 200 µL serum-free DMEM. In another Eppendorf tube, 200 µL serum-free DMEM and 8 µL PEI were mixed, and incubate at room temperature for 10 min. Then, combine the contents of the two tubes and incubate for an additional 20 min. Then, added the mixture to the six-well plate and mix gently. Incubate the plate in the incubator for 6 h, then replace the medium with a complete medium. Fourty-eight hours after transfection, collect the first batch of virus supernatant and add complete medium into the six-well plate. After 24 h, the second virus supernatant was collected. The supernatant should be centrifuge at 350 g for 10 min before infecting mesangial cells. Twenty-four hours before the infection, seeded 2 × 105 cells per well in a six-well plate. Mixed the virus solution with complete medium at a 1:1 ratio (~3 mL) and added it to the wells. After 12 h of infection, the medium was replaced with fresh complete medium. Twelve hours after the replacement with fresh medium, the second infection was performed by adding the mixed virus solution again. Once the cells reached 1 × 108, they were subjected to flow cytometric sorting (excitation wavelength 488 nm, emission wavelength 530 nm, Sony SA3800).
Inhibition of TfR1 in mesangial cells using Ferristatin II

Mesangial cells were cultured in serum-free medium for 6 h and then treated with 50 μM Ferristatin II (Cayman, #36621). Cells were incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO2 for 6 h. PBS was used as the vehicle control.
Detection of protein aggregates in mesangial cells

Detection of aggregates in mesangial cells was conducted using the PROTEOSTAT® Aggresome Detection Kit (ENZ-51035, Enzo). This kit employs a 488 nm excitable red fluorescent dye to detect misfolded proteins within aggresomes. Human mesangial cells were grown on confocal dish to achieve 80% confluency. Cells were treated with 0.5 mg/mL Gd-IgA1 or HC-IgA1 for 4 h before washed by 1 × PBS for three times. Cells treated with PBS alone were served as negative control. Following treatment, cells were washed twice with PBS, and 1000 μL of 4% formaldehyde was applied. The cells were incubated for 30 min at room temperature. After fixation, cells were washed twice with PBS, and 500 μL of permeabilizing solution (0.5% Triton X-100, 3 mM EDTA, pH 8.0) was applied. Following permeabilization, excess buffer was removed, 1 μL of PROTEOSTAT® Aggresome Detection Reagent in 2 mL assay buffer was added to the cover the cells. Samples were protected from light and incubated for 30 min at room temperature. After incubation, the cells were subjected to analysis using a ZEISS LSM 900 confocal microscope, which was set to excite fluorescence at a wavelength of 550 nanometers.
Lysosomal activity assay

To evaluate the effect of Gd-IgA1 on lysosomal function in mesangial cells, we utilized a lysosomal intracellular activity assay kit (Abcam, catalog no. ab234622). In brief, mesangial cells were incubated with media containing either a positive control (10 μM Cytochalasin D), Gd-IgA1 (1 mg/mL), or PBS for 1 h at 37 °C with 5% CO2. Following incubation, the media was discarded and the cells were refreshed with new medium with 5% FBS. Then, 15 µL Self-Quenched substrate was added per milliliter of medium to both experimental and control wells. Cells were further incubated for 1 h at 37 °C with 5% CO2. To terminate the enzymatic reaction, cells were washed twice with 1 mL of ice-cold assay buffer. Finally, the cells were analyzed by flow cytometry using a 488 nm excitation filter.
Multiplex ELISA array of cytokines secreted by mesangial cells

Mesangial cells were incubated with Gd-IgA1 or HC-IgA1 (1 mg/mL) for 24 h. Following this incubation period, the medium was replaced with fresh medium, and the cells were allowed to incubate for an additional 24 h. The conditioned medium was then collected and analyzed using a multiplex ELISA array that included a panel of 120 cytokines (Human Cytokine Array GS2000, RayBiotech Life, Inc.) following the manufacturer’s protocol.
Histology and RNAscope in situ hybridization

Paraffin-embedded human kidney sections (5 μm thickness) were prepared by a routine procedure. RNAscope in situ hybridization were performed using Probe-Hs-TFRC (cat#437351), Probe- Hs-ACTA2 (cat#1083431), and the RNAscope Multiplex Fluorescent V2 Assay kit (all from Advanced Cell Diagnostics, ACD). Slides were baked at 60°C for 30 min. Slides were incubated in xylene for 10 min twice and 100% ethanol for 2 min twice at room temperature. Slides were airdried and incubated with 10% H2O2 for 10 min at room temperature. After rinsing in distilled water three times, slides were incubated in ACD heat retrieval buffer for 5 min at 95 °C. Slides were rinsed in distilled water three times and incubated in 100% ethanol for 3 min at room temperature. Slides were air dried and incubated with plus protease for 30 min at 40 °C in a humidified slide moat. Samples were incubated with RNAscope probes for 2 h at 40 °C. Slides were washed twice in wash buffer for 2 min at room temperature after probe incubation and between each amplification step. Samples were incubated sequentially with Amp1 for 30 min at 40 °C, Amp2 for 30 min at 40 °C, Amp3 for 15 min at 40 °C, HRP-C1 for 15 min at 40 °C, TSA Plus FITC diluted 1:1000 in TSA buffer for 30 min at 40 °C, and HRP blocker for 15 min at 40 °C, HRP-C2 for 15 min at 40 °C, TSA Plus Cy3 diluted 1:1000 in TSA buffer for 30 min at 40 °C, and HRP blocker for 15 min at 40 °C. Images were examined semi-blind by two renal researchers and consensus was reached.
Preparation and characterization of HC-IgA1 and Gd-IgA1

Normal human serum was collected to purify IgA protein. The purification of IgA and Gd-IgA1 was performed as previously described. Briefly, HC-IgA1 was purified from normal human serum. Serum samples of healthy individuals were first diluted with 10 times PBS, and then incubated with Capture SelectTM IgA-CH1 (Hu) affinity matrix (194311010; Thermo Scientific) at 4 °C for 1 h. After that, the beads were collected by a 50 mL gravity column and washed with 60-100 mL PBS. 0.1 M glycine (pH = 3.0). Gd-IgA1 protein was obtained by enzymatic digestion of IgA1 derived from the healthy control, a well-established approach for generating Gd-IgA1. 1 mg of purified IgA1 proteins were treated with 4000 U α2-3,6,8 neuraminidase (P0720L; New England Biolabs), and 400 U β1-3 galactosidase (P0726S; New England Biolabs) in PBS, pH 7.4, at 37 °C for 2 h. Gd-IgA1 was then subjected to dialysis against PBS to remove the glycosidase. The purity of both proteins was assessed using Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining and western blot.

HC-IgA1 and Gd-IgA1 samples were prepared in PBS, pH 7.4. Size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) was performed using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) on a cytiva AKTA pure system, with PBS as the mobile phase at a flow rate of 0.6 mL/min. The column was equilibrated for at least three column volumes at 4°C before injection of 500 μL sample volume. Protein detection was carried out at 280 nm, and fractions were collected manually.

Immunohistochemical staining

Slides were baked at 60 °C for 30 min, then incubated in xylene twice for 15 min each, 100% ethanol for 5 min twice, 95% ethanol for 5 min, 90% ethanol for 5 min, 80% ethanol for 5 min, 75% ethanol for 5 min, 70% ethanol for 5 min, 50% ethanol for 5 min at room temperature slides were incubated in EDTA retrieval buffer (ZLI-9072; Zsbio) for 15 min at 100°C. After washing with distilled water, the slides were incubated with 10% H2O2 for 10 min at room temperature. Following a 30-min blocking step with blocking buffer, the slides were incubated with primary anti-TfR (dilution 1:100; HPA028598; Sigma) overnight at 4 °C, and staining with secondary antibodies (GK600710; Gene Tech) for 1 h at room temperature. The slides were also stained with 3,3’-diaminobenzidine (DAB) to visualize the expression. Visualization was performed using a HAMAMATSU laser scanning microscope.
Western blot analysis

Cells or kidney tissues were lysed on ice with radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer (89900; Thermo scientific) and protease and phosphatase inhibitor (A32961; Thermo scientific) in PBS. The supernatants were collected after centrifugation at 12000 g for 10 min at 4°C. Protein expression was analyzed by western blot analysis. The antibodies used were anti-TfR (dilution 1:1000; ab214039; Abcam), anti-Cathepsin B (dilution 1:1000; 12216-1; Proteintech), anti-Cathepsin D (dilution 1:1000; 21327-1; Proteintech), anti-TFEB (dilution 1:1000; 68632-1; Proteintech), anti-β-actin (dilution 1:5000; 66009-1-Ig; Proteintech) and anti-Rabbit IgG (dilution 1:5000; 111-035-003; Jackson).
Mice model

All animal procedures were in accordance with the guidelines and approved by the Ethics Committee of Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital. Eight-week-old male BALB/c Nude mice were used in this study. Mice were randomly assigned to experimental or control groups with block randomization method. In the overexpression experiment, TfR1 was overexpressed in nude mice by intravenous injection of AAV9-Tfrc or AAV9-CTL virus (2 × 1010 GC/g bodyweight). In the knockdown experiment, TfR1 was knocked down using AAV9-shTfrc or AAV9-shCTL virus (4 × 1010 GC/g bodyweight). Only male mice were used in this study, as the interaction between TfR1 and Gd-IgA1 is not expected to differ significantly between male and female mice. Mice were group-housed under a 12:12 h light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to food and water.
Real-time in vivo fluorescence imaging for evaluating the kinetics of Gd-IgA1

Eight-week-old male BALB/c Nude mice were intravenously administered with 200 μL Indocyanine green (ICG) labeled protein at the concentration of 2.5 mg/mL, and the molar ratio of ICG and protein in the labeling process was 5: 1. Real-time monitoring of the biodistribution of ICG-labeled human Gd- IgA1 was performed by IVIS Spectrum In Vivo Imaging System (Perkin Elmer, USA). The excitation and emission filters are 745 nm and 840 nm, respectively. The exposure time is 2 s. The binning level of the images is 1. Scanning range mode is D (20 × 20 cm2). Fluorescence images of mice were captured before injection and at different time points post-injection. The fluorescence signal of kidney was analyzed by the manufacturer’s quantitative analysis system.
Construct preparations and protein purification

Plasmid construction. Extracellular domain of human TfR1 gene (101-760; Uniprot-P02786) was synthesized and cloned into a pFastbac1 vector by the Anhui General Biol Co. China for TfR1 (TfR1) protein expression. The N-terminal of TfR1 contains a GP67 signal peptide, and C-terminal with 6 × His tag.

The heavy constant α-chain sequence of IgA1 for the CH1, CH2 and CH3 domains was taken from SWISSPROT (Unipro-P01876-1), and heavy variable α-chain domain (VH) and light chain (VL and CL) sequences were taken from the crystal structure of human TR1.9 IgG1 Fab (PDB code: 1vge). For recombinant IgA1 purification, a 3 × Flag tag (DYKDHDGDYKDHDIDYKDDDDKLVPRGS) after the HIV signal peptide (MDAMKRGLCCVLLLCGAVFVSPAGA) was added to the N-terminal of the heavy constant α-chain, as previous reported. Residue numbering is based on the recombinant IgA1 containing an N-terminal FLAG tag.

Recombinant TfR1 expression and purification

Sf9 cells (Spodoptera frugiperda) were cultured in serum-free insect cell culture media (Union-Biotech, UK1000) at 27 °C, 120 round per minute (rpm) and passaged every 2 days and for no more than 20 passages. Bac-viruses were prepared following protocol of the Bac-to-BacTM baculovirus expression system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10359016). Briefly, the pFast bac1 plasmid constructed TfR1 genes were firstly transformed into E. coli strain DH10bac cells for transposition into the bacmid. The recombinant bacmid was isolated and was mixed with cellfectin with regent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10362100), then the mixture was used to transfected sf9 cells for passage 1 recombinant bac-virus (P1 virus) preparation. The P1 virus was then used as seed to amplify the virus stock for another two rounds. Finally, passage 3 (P3) bac-virus was used for protein expression.

For TfR1 expression, sf9 cells were seeded at a density of 2.5 × 106, and 0.25% P3 virus was added. After 3 days suspension culture, the supernatant was collected by 18,000 g centrifugation at 4°C. 2 mL Ni-NTA beads were added to the culture medium, and then incubated by 500 rpm stirring for 2 h at 4°C. All beads were collected by a 50 mL gravity-column, and washed by buffer A (20 mM Hepes, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM DTT) containing gradient concentration of imidazole for 20 mM to 50 mM, and eluted by buffer A containing 250 mM imidazole. The elution was concentrated by a 50 kDa cutoff concentrator and loaded onto a Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva, 29091596) in buffer A. The TfR1 in peaks was collected and freeze quickly by liquid nitrogen and stored in −80°C for further using.
Recombinant IgA1 expression and purification

HEK293F cells was maintained in serum-free mammalian cells culture medium (Union-Biotech, UK1001). To express IgA1 protein, the HEK293F cells was diluted to 2.5 × 106/mL in fresh medium. For IgA1 preparation, plasmids containing equal amount of heavy and light chain were mixed with PEI at a ratio of 1:3 in medium, and added to cell culture for protein expression. In the 20th hour of transfection, 10 mM sodium butyrate was supplemented to enhance protein expression. After 5 days culture, the supernatant was collected by 18,000 g centrifugation at 4°C, and IgA1 proteins were purified from medium by the Flag beads (Genscript, L00432). The elute was concentrated and further purified by a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva, 17517501) in buffer A.
Co-Immunoprecipitation assay

About 50 μg TfR1 protein was incubated with 50 μL Ni-NTA beads in buffer A at room temperature (RT) for 20 mins, and the beads were washed with buffer A for three times to remove unbound protein. Next, 200 μg purified total IgA1 was added to the beads, and the volume was filled to 400 μL with buffer A (pH7.2). The mixture was incubated on a turbosonic at RT for 2 h. After that, a 500 g centrifuge was made to collect the supernatant (flow-through), and using 400 μL buffer A (pH7.2) to wash beads, then made another round of centrifuge to collect washing solution. Repeated washing steps for twice, and added 400 μL elution buffer (buffer A containing 200 mM imidazole) to elute bound proteins, collected the supernatant after centrifugation. 50 μL sample from each step was taken for SDS-PAGE and western Blot analysis.
When pH 5.5 condition was tested, the buffer A (pH 7.2) was replaced by buffer A (pH 5.5), and other operations remained unchanged.
Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assay

Purified TfR1 protein was used for directly detect affinity parameters of TfR1 and various types of Gd-IgA1 or hinge peptides by surface plasmon resonance (SPR). Filtered Hepes buffer (20 mM Hepes, pH7.5, 150 mM NaCl) was used as running buffer throughout the determination. If different pH conditions were tested, the running buffer was replaced and filled the system before starting tests. After the CM5 chip (Cytiva, 29149604) was loaded and cleaned by 50 mM NaOH and activated by EDC/NHS mixture, ~12, 000 RU of TfR1 (0.05 mg/mL diluted in pH4.5 50 mM acetic acid buffer) was captured on channel 2. The channel 1 was untreated and used as reference channel. For the quick binding test, the Gd-IgA1 proteins were diluted to 0.25 μM with selected running buffer, and 1 μM transferrin was used as positive control, and 10 μM BSA and 10 μM β−1.3-galactosidase was used as negative control. The time of samples injection was 120 s, and disassociate 120 s. When peptide ligands were tested, the peptides were diluted to 50 μM for sampling, and 50 μM Flag peptide used as negative control. For kinetic binding test, the ligands were diluted to a series of concentrations for general procedure. Four steps were included, channel washing 60 s, ligand association 120 s, disassociation 480 s and regeneration 120 s, with flow rate 10 μL/min, temperature 25°C. A kinetic analysis of each ligand/analyte interaction was obtained by fitting the response data (containing 6-8 gradients of ligand concentrations) to a 1:1 bimolecular interaction mode (Ka, fit global; Kd, fit global; Ramx, fit global; tc, fit global; R1, constant; Drift, constant).
Liquid Chromatography Tandem Mass Spectrometry

Samples preparation: purified TfR1 protein was mixed with Gd-IgA1 at a molar ratio of 1:3 in buffer A (pH 5.5) and incubated at room temperature for 2 hours. After that, the 1-Ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl) carbodiimide (EDC) and N-Hydroxysulfosuccinimide (sulfo-NHS) solutions (Cytiva, BR100050) were mixed with a ratio of (1:5, v: v) and transferred to the protein mixture at a ratio of (1:10, v: v) drop by drop. The sample continued to incubate under room temperature for another 2 hours, and then equal volume of 100 mM tris buffer (pH 5.5) was used to end the crosslinking reaction. 100 μL samples (about 50-60 μg proteins) were denatured by adding 20 μL 5 × loading buffer and treated in 100 °C heating, and then separated by SDS-PAGE with a gradient gel (4-15%). The Gd-IgA1 and TfR1 crosslinked band in the gel was cut and analyzed by mass spectrometry.

Liquid Chromatography Tandem Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with an High-Energy Collisional Dissociation (HCD) fragmentation function was employed for LC-MS/MS analyses. The gel samples were firstly cut into little pieces ( ~ 1 mm3) and incubated in 50 mM NH4HCO3/acetonitrile solution (1:1, v: v) to destain. Then the gel was washed using 100% acetonitrile for 2 times and dehydrated in vacuum. The samples were treated with DTT and IAA to reductive alkylation. Protein digested using trypsin overnight, and peptides were recollected and concentrated using a vacuum concentrator. In LC-MS/MS analysis, digested products were separated by a 120 min gradient elution at a flow rate 0.300 µL/min with the Thermo Ultimate 3000 nano-UPLC system which was directly interfaced with the Thermo Fusion LUMOS mass spectrometer. The analytical column was an Acclaim PepMap RSLC column (75 µm ID, 250 mm length, C18). Mobile phase A consisted of 0.1% formic acid, and mobile phase B consisted of 100% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid. The Fusion LUMOS mass spectrometer was operated in the data-dependent acquisition mode using Xcalibur 4.1.50 software and there is a single full-scan mass spectrum in the Orbitrap (375−1500 m/z, 60,000 resolution) followed by data-dependent MS/MS scans. The MS/MS spectra from each LC-MS/MS run were searched against the selected database using the software Byonic.
Synthesis of GalNAc modified hinge peptide of IgA1

A 38 mer peptide (-DYKDDDDKGSGSPVPSTPPTPSPSTPPTPSPSCCHPRR-) covering the hinge region of IgA1 was synthesized. This peptide was glycosylated with GalNAc and synthesized on Wang resin from the C-terminus to the N-terminus following solid phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) protocols and was commercially obtained from MedChemExpress. The glycosylated peptide was validated by mass spectrometry.
Statistics

Quantitative data are displayed as mean ± SD. Statistical differences were determined using a Student’s t-test for two groups or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Dunnett’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. Nonparametric data were analyzed by Mann-Whitney test. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS Statistics version 23.
